description: Production-path E2E cases for rag_service.chat(). Mix of realistic user phrasing, multi-condition profiles, and integrated safety checks. References are author-defined gold answers for the LLM judge only.

cases.question: I'm diabetic and work night shifts. What should I eat before and during my shift?
cases.reference: Eat regular balanced meals with non-starchy vegetables, lean protein, and controlled carbohydrates. Plan a small protein-and-fiber snack for the shift. Avoid skipping meals, which can cause blood sugar swings. Drink water instead of sugary drinks.

cases.question: I only have $20 for groceries this week. What should I buy for low-sodium meals?
cases.reference: Focus on budget staples: dried beans, brown rice, frozen vegetables without added salt, eggs, and in-season produce. Choose store brands, plan meals ahead, and limit processed and canned high-sodium foods.

cases.question: Can I eat canned soup if I have diabetes and high blood pressure?
cases.reference: Most canned soups are high in sodium and may spike blood sugar if portions are large. Choose low-sodium or no-salt-added options, check labels, and pair a small portion with vegetables and protein. Limit regular canned soup due to sodium targets for blood pressure.

cases.question: I don't like vegetables. What can I still eat to manage my weight?
cases.reference: Try vegetables prepared differently (roasted, in soups, blended into sauces), fruit, beans, whole grains, and lean protein. Portion control and limiting sugary drinks and processed snacks still matter even if vegetable intake is low.

cases.question: What should I eat for breakfast to keep my blood sugar steady?
cases.reference: A balanced breakfast combines protein, fiber, and controlled carbohydrates. Examples include eggs with vegetables, Greek yogurt with berries and nuts, or oatmeal with nuts. Avoid sugary cereals and juice. The Diabetes Plate approach balances portions.

cases.question: Give me ideas for a low-sodium dinner.
cases.reference: Build a DASH-style dinner with vegetables, a lean protein such as fish or chicken, and a whole grain. Use herbs and spices instead of salt. Limit processed sauces and canned items high in sodium.

cases.question: What can I make for dinner with what I have in my pantry?
cases.reference: Combine broccoli, chicken breast, and brown rice into a balanced plate: non-starchy vegetables, lean protein, and a whole-grain carbohydrate portion. Keep sauces low in sugar and sodium.

cases.question: I was told I have prediabetes. What everyday food changes matter most?
cases.reference: Choose whole grains over refined grains, add fiber, limit sugary drinks and processed snacks, eat regular balanced meals, and aim for modest weight loss of about 5 to 7 percent through healthier eating and activity.

cases.question: Are sports drinks okay when I'm working out with diabetes?
cases.reference: Sports drinks are usually high in sugar and are meant for long intense exercise. Water is the best default for most workouts. People with diabetes should avoid sugary sports drinks unless a care team advises otherwise for a specific situation.

cases.question: I stress eat at night. Any practical tips?
cases.reference: Try mindful eating, planning satisfying meals during the day, keeping trigger snacks out of easy reach, and using protein-and-fiber snacks if hungry. Stress management and consistent sleep also help reduce night eating.
